About the category

Chardonnay is widely planted throughout the world but its traditional home is Burgundy in the east of France, and it fares particularly well in the Côte de Beaune and Chablis where it thrives on the predominantly chalky soils.

It’s relatively easy to grow and winemakers love it for how readily it responds to a variety of techniques. As to what constitutes a good example is hard to define clearly, however. It can vary in colour from very pale to pronounced straw-yellow while it can be steely dry to rather rich and full on the palate. Flavours are often subtle and understated and yet beguiling.

In South Africa, Chardonnay is the seventh most widely planted variety overall, making up 7.6% of the total area under vineyard at the end of 2025.

title: Malu Lambert: Palomino – the grape that refused to die
summary:
“It’s hellishly special in the fact that it’s own-rooted,” says Leon Coetzee, not known to mince words. The post Malu Lambert: Palomino – the grape that refused to die appeared first on winemag.
content:
“It’s hellishly special in the fact that it’s own-rooted,” says Leon Coetzee, not known to mince words. Coetzee is referring to the 1962 vineyard that produces their Klein Karoo Palomino, now in its third vintage with the 2025.

The wine belongs to the Fledge & Co. portfolio, an independent label run by Coetzee and his wife, Margaux Nel. They source fruit from across the Cape, making the wines in the Boplaas cellar, where Margaux is also the sixth-generation winemaker at her family estate.

The pergola trained site growing along the Gamka River, “has seen many droughts, floods and sometimes a good year in the extreme climate of the Klein Karoo”. The vineyard, he says, is on the De Kranz farm, close to the cellar that belonged to Margaux’s family before her great-grandfather died, and where her father, Carel, and Boets later made wine together. The vines grow on sandy alluvial soil over deep red clay.

“The training keeps the vines off the ground so that flood irrigation as well as flooding from the river doesn’t cause too much damage,” explains Coetzee of the ancient system. “It also helps prevent sunburn.

“We are contemplating pergola for alvarinho now too.” The dakke (‘roofs’) are also handy in that pickers are protected from the heat and livestock can graze under the vines.

“The old vines still produce an obscene amount of grapes.” While the majority of fruit gets siphoned off elsewhere, for the Fledge, they make just two 500-litre barrels per vintage, with the remainder of their parcel going into their solera-style white fortified project.

“The fruit never gets super-ripe, even though it’s the last we take in each year. The alcohol hovers around 11 per cent. The last two years have produced fruit with subtle pear flavours and seriously chalky tannins.

“Winemaking is weird and wonderful,” says Coetzee, citing whole-cluster fermentation and some destemming, gentle punch-downs, foot-treading, extended post-ferment maceration and then ageing in old oak for around 16 months. The wine develops a layer of flor, and they bottle directly from cask.

As well as being a workhorse grape, a palomino is also a kind of horse, hence the Fledge’s striking label of a stallion charging through a gold Karoo desert. “The grape is lekker ’70s, so we went with the same aesthetic as a TV tray in Margaux’s gran’s house.”

The vineyard, he says, is due to be grubbed up to make way for muscat. When it goes, they plan to plant a few rows of it at Boplaas.

Just 10,67-hectares (ha) remain in the Klein Karoo.

Ride or die

Once a workhorse of the South African wine industry, palomino has all but been stabled. Said to be one of South Africa’s earliest grape varieties, there is evidence that Fransdruif (French grape), its colloquial Cape name, was present in the 17th century, with some sources suggesting it predates the arrival of Simon van der Stel in 1679.

By 1909, it had a real presence. The name, of course, was incorrect. In the 1920s, Abraham Perold identified the supposedly French grape as Spain’s palomino fino. It became a variety appreciated for high yields and widely used for brandy, sherry-style and inexpensive white wines. As recently as 1981, it still accounted for more than 13,000 ha of vineyard, before chenin and colombar increasingly displaced it.

By 2025, just 91.4 ha remained, a collapse of more than 99 per cent. Around 96% of those vines are more than 20 years old, with 80.92 ha declared as Old Vine.

Many of these old vines are found in the Piekenierskloof, a treasure trove of ungrafted, pre-phylloxera sites. Though famed for grenache and chenin, increasingly special bottles of palomino are popping up: Dan Colombo’s Agape and Piekenierskloof Platklip Palomino Old Vine spring to mind.

It was also in the Piekenierskloof that Fairview rediscovered palomino too, for the Bloemcool Ploegperd, a blend also including chenin and grenache blanc. Charles Back remembers pulling out his Paarl estate’s old palomino bushvines, once used for KWV sherry. “If I knew what I knew today, I certainly would have kept a block.”

Palomino-philes

Though such sites are rarities, the majority of South Africa’s palomino is still found in the Olifants River (44.22 ha), followed, perhaps surprisingly, by the Swartland (22.80 ha). Here, Eben Sadie can be widely credited with making the grape interesting again through wines such as ’T Voetpad, an ancient Piketberg field blend, and of course, the celebrated Skerpioen.

“I was blown away the first time I saw the vineyard,” says Sadie reflecting on when he saw the garrulous, old bushvines sprawling over white sand. Located in a satellite ward of the Swartland, St. Helena Bay, the Old Vine registry estimates it was planted in 1963.

“Rosa Kruger introduced me to the vineyard. I knew it existed, as many people from the West Coast knew about the witblits made from the vineyard, but I had no idea about its potential. The magic is that it’s co-planted to chenin and palomino, which complement each other in the limestone soils.”

The soils, combined with the cooling Atlantic fog and underground aquifers, are what prompted Sadie and consulting viticulturist Jaco Engelbrecht to start a planting programme here in 2019. Currently, the 6.5 ha includes chenin blanc, vermentino, verdejo, assyrtiko, bastardo do castello, grenache blanc, grenache noir, cinsault and, yes, palomino. Though he cautions that plantings of the grape are minimal, “It’s always going to be a niche thing.

Swartland contemporary Adi Badenhorst has a theory as to why palomino is still so widespread in the area: “No one could afford to uproot the vines,” he laughs. “The vines are old, but they still produce an uncomfortable quantity of fruit.”

Badenhorst bottles ‘Sout van die Aarde’ from the same West Coast vineyard. He also sources palomino from several sites, including his home farm, for fortified wines at The Saldanha Wine & Spirit Co, his sherry-style ‘bodega’ in an old gasoline-pink filling station.

Casting a wider view, Badenhorst says, “It’s certainly on the wane worldwide too, especially in its spiritual home of Jerez. Once a staple of the SA industry, it’s lost ground to tractors of the grape world. No doubt palomino makes some of the finest food wines on the planet and has, of course, been championed by a few producers worldwide. The wines of Envínate, Luis Pérez and Ramiro Ibáñez are household names amongst the world’s palomino-philes for the intriguing and complex wines they produce from this grape.

He says they are still planting “a bit of Vaalblaar”, another colloquialism, this one meaning ‘pale green’, referring to the leaf’s dusty-green appearance.

“We are also,” he says, burying the lead, “propagating a South African crossing of palomino and colombard. This is called, wait for it … colomino.” Crossed by Pall Steyn in 1978, it “from our early trials, contains and expresses the finest traits of these two varieties.”

Colomino, folks. You heard it here first.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

title: Tim James: Why do we drink? And why do I?

The post Tim James: Why do we drink? And why do I? appeared first on winemag.
content:
We all drink alcohol, it’s surely fair to say (unless there are some teetotal voyeurs – liseurs? – reading
this; “we” being the readers, extended to “people generally”). But why? That’s my first question, and
it’s easier to answer, strangely enough, in the first person plural: why do we (human beings) drink
alcohol, than it is in the first person singular: why do I (this particular human being) drink alcohol?

The harder, messier bit I shall return to later. As to why people drink alcohol (to the despair of many,
including the World Health Organisation, which says it’s an unsafe practice at any level of
consumption) – well, I’m convinced by the answers summarised and articulated by Canadian
philosopher Edward Slingerland in his 2021 book called Drunk (subtitled How we sipped, danced, and
stumbled our way to civilization).

I’ve just re-read the book, which I reviewed mostly favourably back in 2023 – have a look there if you
didn’t see it and would like to know more of Slingerland’s arguments and marshalling of the evidence.
Basically, he confronts two facts: first, the overwhelmingly widespread use of alcohol (ahead of a
range of other intoxicants) throughout human history; and, second, the often appalling effects of
alcohol abuse in at least modern society, abuse that’s both social and individual. Given the latter, why
did human evolution allow for and even encourage the former? Why have many governmental
attempts to prohibit its usage seemed doomed to fail?

Because, Slingerland argues (with recourse to everything from pre-history to the structure of the brain
– the need to “dial down the prefrontal cortex”), intoxicants have been crucial to the development of
humans as creative, cultural and communal animals – as well as providing us with comfort and
pleasure.

That’s a very brief summary of his conclusions. As I wrote in my original review, I was convinced by
this argument, and also accepted his uncompromising description of the “dark side of Dionysis” that
seems to have emerged comparatively recently in human history.

Given this evolutionary usefulness, why are there a few societies that don’t have recourse to alcohol,
cannabis, peyote buttons and other hallucinogens and psychedelics? (It seems to have been only
North America where there was historically no use of nature’s escapist and bonding bounty.) This
needs local investigation, which usually reveals other social equivalents – religious ecstasy and
bonding and the like (Trump’s MAGA rallies, perhaps, it occurs to me, in puritanical America).

Fair enough, and that leaves only the question about individual participation or avoidance in drinking.
We here probably know more imbibers than total abstainers, but I’m sure we know some of those.
And we know in some cases that they they are there because they have been badly damaged by
over-indulgence (another recent re-read of mine has been A A Gill’s splendid autobiographical book
Pour Me, which rather entertainingly details the hell of his addiction before he went straight). And we
know in some cases of the substitutes people have. Many people don’t even seem to manage to be
miserable bastards without the occasional drink.

In fact, one of the most excoriated categories of alcohol consumer these days is the solitary drinker –
unaffected, as Slingerland argues, by the subtle social controls generally exercised by communal
consumption, on a large level as still lingers on in cultures like those of the European Mediteranean
countries, or the dining table or pub everywhere. Google the category and you find any number of
warnings, and the images show a lot of the truly miserable, lonely bastards (mostly men) huddled
over their glass or bottle.

I myself do a significant proportion of my wine-drinking solo, almost inevitably around my evening
meal. Worse, these days it usually includes a bit of brandy – and the advent of distillation, giving
unprecedentedly alcohol drinks, is something Slingerland (and no doubt many others) gives some
blame to regarding modern society’s alcohol problems. So perhaps the obvious answer to the
question of why I drink is simply that I’m an old drunk (in the company of the larger part of the wine
industry, in my experience – where usually it’s communal rather than solitary wine-drinking that
obtains, sometimes to the point of leaving me aghast – and comparatively sober).

It doesn’t feel like being simply an old drunk from the inside, and I haven’t had to deal with many
accusations. I seldom get obviously drunk, I’d say, either with others or alone, but admittedly
sometimes there’s more of a buzz than at others, and I certainly enjoy a degree of the buzz. I have
also frequently found that I’m more creative when the buzz is on. I tend to then write a bit more
loosely and uninhibitedly and thoughts flow more interestingly, to the writing’s benefit – though I have
learnt that it’s wise to check my spelling and syntax the next morning. But that’s not a reason, more an
occasional side-benefit. Good wine is pretty delicious and interesting once you’ve got the taste for it,
of course, and that is obviously part of the reason. But probably not all that much more seriously so
than the great world of tea, for example, though more extensive and various.

In the old days of my comparative youth, when I heard of someone’s disease of whatever kind
demanding the total cessation of alcohol consumption I would shudder with horror at the very idea.
Strangely, perhaps, now I think I could cope without alcohol – though I would most certainly not do so
willingly. It seems such an important part of my mealtime, whether a simple or more complex wine
and/or meal. Could I imagine doing as – still, apparently – many American adults and children do, and
have milk or “soda” with my meal? I think not. Or just water? (The aforementioned AA Gill managed,
after all, to be a serious restaurant critic after renouncing alcohol.) Beer, though, can be great,
including my beloved no-alc version Devils Peak Hero. Which reminds me, no also to no-alc wine until
it improves a whole lot (see Jamie Goode’s current piece). Wine, proper wine, retains its supreme
place, even – or arguably especially – for the solitary diner.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine
summary:
A few years back (2009) I was enlisted by a wine company specializing in lower alcohol wines, for me to give them some market support. The post Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine appeared first on winemag.
content:
A few years back (2009) I was enlisted by a wine company specializing in lower alcohol wines, for me to give them some market support. As someone with a technical background, but also a consumer-focused newspaper column, I was potentially useful to them. The owner was a Brit based in California who had worked with the spinning cone, a high-tech way of removing alcohol from wine. He was interesting to work with, although he did have an alarming habit of losing his temper in meetings and slamming his forearm down on the table with more force than was strictly necessary.

I liked the idea. It wasn’t zero-alcohol wine, but wines at perhaps 8% or 5% alcohol, with the proper flavour of wine but less booziness. And with the spinning cone column, they were well placed to make these wines, and benefit from others who saw a market opportunity here.

So after some activity in the UK, I flew to their headquarters in California, where I saw the spinning cone in action, and tasted some of their products. Particularly informative was a tasting where we looked at the same wine at different alcohol levels.

The idea was to start with a wine such as a Chardonnay at 14% alcohol. You take 10 000 litres, which you put through the spinning cone, taking off first the volatile fraction (‘essence’) and then the alcohol, leaving you with 8 250 litres of Chardonnay at 4% alcohol. You then add the aromatic ‘essence’ back in, and the resulting 4% wine can be used as a blending component to add to untreated wine, to result in a final wine at a lower alcohol level.

How did the wines taste? I started off looking at a Californian Chardonnay at 14.3% alcohol. It had a sweet, ripe, slightly buttery nose, leading to a rich buttery palate that was quite broad. I then tasted the same wine after it had been through the spinning cone column, at 4% alcohol. This was more minerally with tangerine notes and some spicy richness. The palate was lemony and tart with hollow fruit and an enhanced sensation of acidity. Their winemaker told me that alcohol is a masking agent so taking it away reveals what’s there. It also adds sweetness to the palate. Also, the acidity is concentrated, and appears higher up in the mix. I guess what this showed is that it really matters what you start off with, when you start taking alcohol out. But also that it has a huge effect on flavour.

The next wine was a blend of 10% of the 4% sample with the remainder of the original wine, resulting in a Chardonnay at 13.2%. This was fresher than the original with more acidity apparent. The fruit showed through more. There was quite a difference, and the 13.2% wine was much nicer than the 14.3% original.

I then tried four different Californian wines each at three alcohol levels: the original level, and then reduced levels of 11% and 8%. A Chardonnay that tasted sweet and buttery at 14% alcohol tasted fresher with nice definition at 11%, and then more lemony and refreshing at 8%. A rosé showed best at 12.2%, and was perhaps less successful at 8%. A Shiraz was sweet, juicy and spicy at 14.6%, but fresher and more vivid with less sweetness at 11%; at 8% it was more savoury with fresh, pure fruit and a more gastronomic character. A Merlot showed really well at 11% and fresh, juicy and bracing with more apparent acidity at 8%. These are inexpensive wines, but with this alcohol reduction they really showed very well.

What was immediately apparent was the role that alcohol has in shaping the flavour and aroma of the wine. Take just a little out, and you have a different wine. But in the region of 8% alcohol and above, you can make some very interesting wines, depending on your starting wine.

But my experience of zero alcohol wine has been quite different. Remove it all, and you have something that really doesn’t taste all that wine like at all. This is for three reasons. First, the alcohol itself is contributing something important to the flavour. It adds some sweetness and richness, and quite a lot of the body. And second, alcohol is acting as a masking agent. We like wines the way they taste, but without alcohol and its masking, suddenly you reveal all sorts of aromas that you didn’t see before. And it smells and tastes different, and a bit weird.

It’s not possible to neatly take off all the aroma compounds in one fraction, then take off the alcohol in a second, and then combine back the aroma compounds. This is because many of the desirable aroma compounds leave in the alcohol stream. The evidence in the scientific literature shows that many of the interesting aroma compounds are lost in the dealcoholization process.

Also, there are significant changes in acidity. For example, one study showed that a white wine where the original level was 6.88 g/L rose to 10.05 g/L in the dealcoholized wine and pH lowers with this from 3.00 to 2.70). This is taking these parameters out of the normal range for table wines.

With much more work on technology, it may be possible to preserve more of the aroma molecules in the wine than is currently possible. But this won’t overcome the second, larger problem faced by non-alcoholic wines – the importance of the non-volatile matrix on aroma release.

But for now, it seems that eliminating alcohol changes so much in a wine that it’s very hard to end up with anything that tastes like wine. For most zero-alcohol wines, it’s normal to add sugar at a level of around 40 g/litre, and the resulting wine doesn’t taste sweet, largely because of the sky-high acidity. But this sort of ultraprocessed wine is sort of at odds with where we are heading in terms of gastronomy at the moment.

I remain optimistic about wines that have just a little alcohol reduced, though. Going from 15% to 12% might be a good thing, or going from 13% to 10%, especially for more commercial styles. Sometimes, picking earlier does this job without intervention. But I’m open to some intervention if the results are good.

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.

content:
The 42nd Cape Winemakers Guild Auction, held on 2 and 3 October, generated R18.22m in sales, up 5.9% on 2025. There were 2,220 cases sold, versus 1,912 last year, an increase of 16%. In other words, more wine shifted and more money raised, but the average price per bottle fell from R1,501 to R1,368.

Hosted by Strauss & Co, the hybrid event (bids accepted in person, online and by telephone) drew 263 registered bidders from 16 countries. 58 wines were offered: 34 reds (1,364 cases), 22 whites (780 cases) and two Cap Classiques (76 cases).

For the first time in the Guild’s 42-year history, white wines, including Cap Classique, achieved a higher average price than reds: R1,416 per bottle versus R1,340, excluding VAT. Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay accounted for 65% of the white wines offered.

The five producers achieving the highest six-bottle-equivalent hammer prices were:

  1. Mullineux The Gris Old Vine Sémillon 2025 – R27,500
  2. Rall Wines Noa Syrah 2024 – R19,000
  3. Leeu Passant Hillside Cabernet Franc 2023 – R17,500
  4. Solo Wines by Carl Schultz CWG Auction Merlot 2023 – R15,000
  5. Van Loggerenberg Wines CWG Auction Syrah 2025 – R13,000

The 96 successful bidders included two private clients among the top 10 buyers, alongside Grootbos, Singita and UK merchant Bordeaux Index.

South African bidders accounted for 78% of sales, the balance hailing from 10 other countries: the UK, Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Hong Kong, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Guernsey and Australia; UK bidders accounted for 7% of the total.

Trade represented just under 30% of bidders but accounted for 44% of the total value purchased.

Separately, the Cape Winemakers Guild Protégé Auction raised R655,900 through donated wines and wine-related experiences. The money supports the Guild’s Protégé Programme, which provides placements and training for emerging South African winemakers.

title: Greg Sherwood MW: The evidence for 2021’s greatness keeps mounting
summary:

The post Greg Sherwood MW: The evidence for 2021’s greatness keeps mounting appeared first on winemag.
content:
In my previous Winemag column, I profiled a wonderful selection of 2021 Cabernet Sauvignons presented in London recently by the Cabernet Collective. Bordeaux-style blends are not normally included in these tastings, but on this occasion a special add-on was offered, many of the UK’s most influential trade and media figures in attendance. 

With favourable comparisons already being made with the iconic 2015 and 2017 vintages, the 2021 reds are looking like prime candidates for a place in the cellars of serious collectors.

Whether you’re an aspiring collector already on a stretched budget in these tough economic times or a fortunate experienced collector (with no doubt far too much wine in your cellar already!) the case can still be made for purchasing a case or two of the exceptional 2021 reds – the Cabernet Sauvignons or Cape Bordeaux Blends.

Stellenbosch’s top Cape Bordeaux blends have done the hard yards over the past decades to earn their global reputation through a rare combination of place, pedigree, and textural polish. Cabernet Sauvignon typically leads, supported by Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, and sometimes Malbec, the style sitting between Old World restraint and New World generosity, which is why collectors in Europe and the USA increasingly treat these wines as serious alternatives to classified growth Bordeaux, often available at a fraction of the price, quality considered.

What makes Stellenbosch Blends exceptional

The region’s advantage begins with geology and geography. Its soils range from decomposed granite on the Simonsberg and Helderberg slopes to weathered Table Mountain sandstone and ancient Malmesbury shale. These soils drain well and stress the vines in a healthy way, producing small berries with concentrated flavour and fine-grained tannins. Altitude and aspect matter just as much. Vineyards on mountain slopes catch cooling breezes from False Bay, and the afternoon “Cape Doctor” wind slows ripening and preserves the all-important acidity.

Then there is the district’s sheer age. Stellenbosch has been making wine since the 17th century, and its best estates now combine old-vine material, refined cellar practices, and a younger generation of winemakers who increasingly favour precision over extraction. Oak is used with far more restraint, alcohol levels are better managed through viticulture and winemaking, and blending decisions are made for harmony rather than power. The result is wines with a distinctly cassis-laden, graphite-tinged depth, an ever-present savoury thread of tobacco leaf and dried herbs, and importantly, the structure and acidity to age beneficially for several decades even in ‘lighter’ vintages.

Why 2021 stands out

Vintage character is what separates good years from legendary ones, and 2021 shows several hallmarks associated with the Cape’s greatest vintages. Adequate winter rainfall replenished soils after the punishing drought years, and a notably cool, moderate growing season followed. Ripening was slow and late, with harvest arriving a couple of weeks behind recent norms. That extended hang time allowed phenolic ripeness to develop fully while sugars stayed in check.

The effect on the wines is significant. Early impressions at five years from vintage point to bright, vibrant fruit profiles, pronounced fragrant aromatic lift, and fresh natural acidities. The tannins are ripe but fine-grained and tightly interwoven, and the alcohol levels are crucially moderate, lending the wines a very European sensibility.

This profile echoes what made the 2015 and 2017 wines so admired: balance, tension, and a sense of effortless concentration rather than brute force. Where 2015 offered classical poise with muscular power and 2017 delivered concentrated, polished wines with harmony and weightless intensity, 2021 appears to blend both qualities with extra freshness. Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon, in particular, seem to have benefited, showing incredible perfume and clarity in the wines.

As always, quality varies site by site as well as by producer, with the finest wines coming from estates with older vines, well-placed mountain parcels with altitude, as well as a steady, experienced guiding hand in the cellar. Collectors should also remember that some critical assessments of a vintage evolve as wines mature in bottle. Still, the early signs at five years on, are strong, and the combination of structure, tension and freshness suggests excellent aging potential, likely 15 to 25+ years for the best examples.

Stellenbosch’s Cape Bordeaux blends already offer an extraordinary mix of terroir, tradition, and value. If the 2021 vintage lives up to its currently assessed promise, it will further cement their standing among the world’s great age-worthy reds, and it will be a vintage worth securing for the cellar before the market catches up, as it has already done so with the 2015s and 2017s.

My Top 2021 Cape Bordeaux Blends from Stellenbosch:

Kanonkop Paul Sauer 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 13.49% Abv.

All the hall mark signs of class are present, minerality, perfumed violets and pink musk, tilled loam and saline black currants. Mouth filling yet supple and seductive, lithe and elegant with the pithy Granitic minerality prominent before a cool, grippy, powerful sinewy finish. True class and certainly one for the cellar! 98/100 GSMW

Glenelly Lady May 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.5% Abv.

Cool, dark fruited and precise, showing beautiful saline hints, crème de cassis, maritime kelp, violets, dried herbs and potpourri. Seductive and chalky in the mouth, this is a real beauty, harmonious, powerful, intense yet enticing with majestic balance. 97+/100 GSMW

Thelema Rabelais 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.5% Abv.

This is a serious wine and predictably it’s starting to tighten up and close down somewhat. The aromatics are Granitic and dusty with hints of graphite, Sichuan pepper and earthy black currant. Despite the tension, the palate is sleek, chiselled and beautifully precise with marble-like tannins, bright tangy acids and a focused, powerfully juicy finish. Undoubtedly one of the blends of the vintage. 97+/100 GSMW

Meerlust Rubicon 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.2% Abv.

A cool earthy expression loaded with black currant, tea leaves, wet tobacco and a coastal maritime kelpy salinity. The tannins are stony and mineral, the palate tense and nervy, perhaps getting ready for a broader shut down for a few years. This is a top league Rubicon that will need to be left in the cellar for a few years. Supremely classy, this will rival the iconic 2015 in time! 96+/100 GSMW

Ernie Els Signature 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 13.5% Abv.

Reveals exotic black fruited aromatics with a cool precision, a pinpoint purity, saline black berry fruits and subtle kelp notes. The palate is incredibly tight knit and polished, showing powdery silky tannins, a nervy acidity and a majestic balance. This has class written all over it. 96/100 GSMW

Rust en Vrede Estate 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.4% Abv.

Not strictly a Bordeaux-style blend but close enough. A deliciously opulent black fruited aromatics show cool creamy crème de cassis hints, black cherry kirsch liquor and subtle saline maritime notes. The texture is accessible and plush, silky, fine grained and luxurious underpinned by stony mineral tannins. A South African classic. 95+/100 GSMW

Cavalli Warlord 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.14% Abv.

Beautiful lift and perfume with exotic notes of black cherry kirsch liquor, salty black currant, hints of liquorice and subtle maritime saline hints. Super plush and sleek, fine grained, fleshy but beautifully elegant. A very well-made classy expression indeed with great appeal. 95+/100 GSMW

Journey’s End Cape Doctor 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.5% Abv.

Classical sweet sappy Cabernet notes shine with black currant, wet tobacco leaf, graphite and sappy cedar spice. Finely weighted palate, an enlivening freshness and cool, plush layers of blue and black berry fruits and supple chalky tannins in support. Really very impressive. 95+/100 GSMW

Klein Graniet Tribute 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14% Abv.

Deep fleshy black fruits shine on the nose with a kiss of salted liquorice, tilled earth and savoury black currant. The palate is chalky and soft, furry tannins coating the mouth. Plenty of power and grip on display, so give this time to unfurl fully. 94/100 GSMW

Le Grand Domaine Grand Vin de Stellenbosch 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 14.6% Abv.

The cool, creamy lactic aromatics suggest black berry chocolate gateau, salted toffee and delicate iodine notes. The palate is soft and supple, quite earthy with tilled loam, black currant and cold brewed tea tannins. Closing up a bit now so give this time. 93+/100 GSMW

Waterford Antigo 2021, WO Stellenbosch, 13.3% Abv.

This Cabernet heavy blend shows layers of black currant, crème de cassis, black cherry and subtle dry bushveld and fynbos herbal nuances. Plush, sleek and accessible, this is a more approachable expression with supple tannins and an effortlessly generous finish. Good to go now. 92+/100 GSMW

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

content:
“It’s hellishly special in the fact that it’s own-rooted,” says Leon Coetzee, not known to mince words. Coetzee is referring to the 1962 vineyard that produces their Klein Karoo Palomino, now in its third vintage with the 2025.

The wine belongs to the Fledge & Co. portfolio, an independent label run by Coetzee and his wife, Margaux Nel. They source fruit from across the Cape, making the wines in the Boplaas cellar, where Margaux is also the sixth-generation winemaker at her family estate.

The pergola trained site growing along the Gamka River, “has seen many droughts, floods and sometimes a good year in the extreme climate of the Klein Karoo”. The vineyard, he says, is on the De Kranz farm, close to the cellar that belonged to Margaux’s family before her great-grandfather died, and where her father, Carel, and Boets later made wine together. The vines grow on sandy alluvial soil over deep red clay.

“The training keeps the vines off the ground so that flood irrigation as well as flooding from the river doesn’t cause too much damage,” explains Coetzee of the ancient system. “It also helps prevent sunburn.

“We are contemplating pergola for alvarinho now too.” The dakke (‘roofs’) are also handy in that pickers are protected from the heat and livestock can graze under the vines.

“The old vines still produce an obscene amount of grapes.” While the majority of fruit gets siphoned off elsewhere, for the Fledge, they make just two 500-litre barrels per vintage, with the remainder of their parcel going into their solera-style white fortified project.

“The fruit never gets super-ripe, even though it’s the last we take in each year. The alcohol hovers around 11 per cent. The last two years have produced fruit with subtle pear flavours and seriously chalky tannins.

“Winemaking is weird and wonderful,” says Coetzee, citing whole-cluster fermentation and some destemming, gentle punch-downs, foot-treading, extended post-ferment maceration and then ageing in old oak for around 16 months. The wine develops a layer of flor, and they bottle directly from cask.

As well as being a workhorse grape, a palomino is also a kind of horse, hence the Fledge’s striking label of a stallion charging through a gold Karoo desert. “The grape is lekker ’70s, so we went with the same aesthetic as a TV tray in Margaux’s gran’s house.”

The vineyard, he says, is due to be grubbed up to make way for muscat. When it goes, they plan to plant a few rows of it at Boplaas.

Just 10,67-hectares (ha) remain in the Klein Karoo.

Ride or die

Once a workhorse of the South African wine industry, palomino has all but been stabled. Said to be one of South Africa’s earliest grape varieties, there is evidence that Fransdruif (French grape), its colloquial Cape name, was present in the 17th century, with some sources suggesting it predates the arrival of Simon van der Stel in 1679.

By 1909, it had a real presence. The name, of course, was incorrect. In the 1920s, Abraham Perold identified the supposedly French grape as Spain’s palomino fino. It became a variety appreciated for high yields and widely used for brandy, sherry-style and inexpensive white wines. As recently as 1981, it still accounted for more than 13,000 ha of vineyard, before chenin and colombar increasingly displaced it.

By 2025, just 91.4 ha remained, a collapse of more than 99 per cent. Around 96% of those vines are more than 20 years old, with 80.92 ha declared as Old Vine.

Many of these old vines are found in the Piekenierskloof, a treasure trove of ungrafted, pre-phylloxera sites. Though famed for grenache and chenin, increasingly special bottles of palomino are popping up: Dan Colombo’s Agape and Piekenierskloof Platklip Palomino Old Vine spring to mind.

It was also in the Piekenierskloof that Fairview rediscovered palomino too, for the Bloemcool Ploegperd, a blend also including chenin and grenache blanc. Charles Back remembers pulling out his Paarl estate’s old palomino bushvines, once used for KWV sherry. “If I knew what I knew today, I certainly would have kept a block.”

Palomino-philes

Though such sites are rarities, the majority of South Africa’s palomino is still found in the Olifants River (44.22 ha), followed, perhaps surprisingly, by the Swartland (22.80 ha). Here, Eben Sadie can be widely credited with making the grape interesting again through wines such as ’T Voetpad, an ancient Piketberg field blend, and of course, the celebrated Skerpioen.

“I was blown away the first time I saw the vineyard,” says Sadie reflecting on when he saw the garrulous, old bushvines sprawling over white sand. Located in a satellite ward of the Swartland, St. Helena Bay, the Old Vine registry estimates it was planted in 1963.

“Rosa Kruger introduced me to the vineyard. I knew it existed, as many people from the West Coast knew about the witblits made from the vineyard, but I had no idea about its potential. The magic is that it’s co-planted to chenin and palomino, which complement each other in the limestone soils.”

The soils, combined with the cooling Atlantic fog and underground aquifers, are what prompted Sadie and consulting viticulturist Jaco Engelbrecht to start a planting programme here in 2019. Currently, the 6.5 ha includes chenin blanc, vermentino, verdejo, assyrtiko, bastardo do castello, grenache blanc, grenache noir, cinsault and, yes, palomino. Though he cautions that plantings of the grape are minimal, “It’s always going to be a niche thing.

Swartland contemporary Adi Badenhorst has a theory as to why palomino is still so widespread in the area: “No one could afford to uproot the vines,” he laughs. “The vines are old, but they still produce an uncomfortable quantity of fruit.”

Badenhorst bottles ‘Sout van die Aarde’ from the same West Coast vineyard. He also sources palomino from several sites, including his home farm, for fortified wines at The Saldanha Wine & Spirit Co, his sherry-style ‘bodega’ in an old gasoline-pink filling station.

Casting a wider view, Badenhorst says, “It’s certainly on the wane worldwide too, especially in its spiritual home of Jerez. Once a staple of the SA industry, it’s lost ground to tractors of the grape world. No doubt palomino makes some of the finest food wines on the planet and has, of course, been championed by a few producers worldwide. The wines of Envínate, Luis Pérez and Ramiro Ibáñez are household names amongst the world’s palomino-philes for the intriguing and complex wines they produce from this grape.

He says they are still planting “a bit of Vaalblaar”, another colloquialism, this one meaning ‘pale green’, referring to the leaf’s dusty-green appearance.

“We are also,” he says, burying the lead, “propagating a South African crossing of palomino and colombard. This is called, wait for it … colomino.” Crossed by Pall Steyn in 1978, it “from our early trials, contains and expresses the finest traits of these two varieties.”

Colomino, folks. You heard it here first.

She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

content:
We all drink alcohol, it’s surely fair to say (unless there are some teetotal voyeurs – liseurs? – reading
this; “we” being the readers, extended to “people generally”). But why? That’s my first question, and
it’s easier to answer, strangely enough, in the first person plural: why do we (human beings) drink
alcohol, than it is in the first person singular: why do I (this particular human being) drink alcohol?

The harder, messier bit I shall return to later. As to why people drink alcohol (to the despair of many,
including the World Health Organisation, which says it’s an unsafe practice at any level of
consumption) – well, I’m convinced by the answers summarised and articulated by Canadian
philosopher Edward Slingerland in his 2021 book called Drunk (subtitled How we sipped, danced, and
stumbled our way to civilization).

I’ve just re-read the book, which I reviewed mostly favourably back in 2023 – have a look there if you
didn’t see it and would like to know more of Slingerland’s arguments and marshalling of the evidence.
Basically, he confronts two facts: first, the overwhelmingly widespread use of alcohol (ahead of a
range of other intoxicants) throughout human history; and, second, the often appalling effects of
alcohol abuse in at least modern society, abuse that’s both social and individual. Given the latter, why
did human evolution allow for and even encourage the former? Why have many governmental
attempts to prohibit its usage seemed doomed to fail?

Because, Slingerland argues (with recourse to everything from pre-history to the structure of the brain
– the need to “dial down the prefrontal cortex”), intoxicants have been crucial to the development of
humans as creative, cultural and communal animals – as well as providing us with comfort and
pleasure.

That’s a very brief summary of his conclusions. As I wrote in my original review, I was convinced by
this argument, and also accepted his uncompromising description of the “dark side of Dionysis” that
seems to have emerged comparatively recently in human history.

Given this evolutionary usefulness, why are there a few societies that don’t have recourse to alcohol,
cannabis, peyote buttons and other hallucinogens and psychedelics? (It seems to have been only
North America where there was historically no use of nature’s escapist and bonding bounty.) This
needs local investigation, which usually reveals other social equivalents – religious ecstasy and
bonding and the like (Trump’s MAGA rallies, perhaps, it occurs to me, in puritanical America).

Fair enough, and that leaves only the question about individual participation or avoidance in drinking.
We here probably know more imbibers than total abstainers, but I’m sure we know some of those.
And we know in some cases that they they are there because they have been badly damaged by
over-indulgence (another recent re-read of mine has been A A Gill’s splendid autobiographical book
Pour Me, which rather entertainingly details the hell of his addiction before he went straight). And we
know in some cases of the substitutes people have. Many people don’t even seem to manage to be
miserable bastards without the occasional drink.

In fact, one of the most excoriated categories of alcohol consumer these days is the solitary drinker –
unaffected, as Slingerland argues, by the subtle social controls generally exercised by communal
consumption, on a large level as still lingers on in cultures like those of the European Mediteranean
countries, or the dining table or pub everywhere. Google the category and you find any number of
warnings, and the images show a lot of the truly miserable, lonely bastards (mostly men) huddled
over their glass or bottle.

I myself do a significant proportion of my wine-drinking solo, almost inevitably around my evening
meal. Worse, these days it usually includes a bit of brandy – and the advent of distillation, giving
unprecedentedly alcohol drinks, is something Slingerland (and no doubt many others) gives some
blame to regarding modern society’s alcohol problems. So perhaps the obvious answer to the
question of why I drink is simply that I’m an old drunk (in the company of the larger part of the wine
industry, in my experience – where usually it’s communal rather than solitary wine-drinking that
obtains, sometimes to the point of leaving me aghast – and comparatively sober).

It doesn’t feel like being simply an old drunk from the inside, and I haven’t had to deal with many
accusations. I seldom get obviously drunk, I’d say, either with others or alone, but admittedly
sometimes there’s more of a buzz than at others, and I certainly enjoy a degree of the buzz. I have
also frequently found that I’m more creative when the buzz is on. I tend to then write a bit more
loosely and uninhibitedly and thoughts flow more interestingly, to the writing’s benefit – though I have
learnt that it’s wise to check my spelling and syntax the next morning. But that’s not a reason, more an
occasional side-benefit. Good wine is pretty delicious and interesting once you’ve got the taste for it,
of course, and that is obviously part of the reason. But probably not all that much more seriously so
than the great world of tea, for example, though more extensive and various.

In the old days of my comparative youth, when I heard of someone’s disease of whatever kind
demanding the total cessation of alcohol consumption I would shudder with horror at the very idea.
Strangely, perhaps, now I think I could cope without alcohol – though I would most certainly not do so
willingly. It seems such an important part of my mealtime, whether a simple or more complex wine
and/or meal. Could I imagine doing as – still, apparently – many American adults and children do, and
have milk or “soda” with my meal? I think not. Or just water? (The aforementioned AA Gill managed,
after all, to be a serious restaurant critic after renouncing alcohol.) Beer, though, can be great,
including my beloved no-alc version Devils Peak Hero. Which reminds me, no also to no-alc wine until
it improves a whole lot (see Jamie Goode’s current piece). Wine, proper wine, retains its supreme
place, even – or arguably especially – for the solitary diner.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine

The post Jamie Goode: Zero-alcohol wine has a problem – it doesn’t taste like wine appeared first on winemag.
content:
A few years back (2009) I was enlisted by a wine company specializing in lower alcohol wines, for me to give them some market support. As someone with a technical background, but also a consumer-focused newspaper column, I was potentially useful to them. The owner was a Brit based in California who had worked with the spinning cone, a high-tech way of removing alcohol from wine. He was interesting to work with, although he did have an alarming habit of losing his temper in meetings and slamming his forearm down on the table with more force than was strictly necessary.

I liked the idea. It wasn’t zero-alcohol wine, but wines at perhaps 8% or 5% alcohol, with the proper flavour of wine but less booziness. And with the spinning cone column, they were well placed to make these wines, and benefit from others who saw a market opportunity here.

So after some activity in the UK, I flew to their headquarters in California, where I saw the spinning cone in action, and tasted some of their products. Particularly informative was a tasting where we looked at the same wine at different alcohol levels.

The idea was to start with a wine such as a Chardonnay at 14% alcohol. You take 10 000 litres, which you put through the spinning cone, taking off first the volatile fraction (‘essence’) and then the alcohol, leaving you with 8 250 litres of Chardonnay at 4% alcohol. You then add the aromatic ‘essence’ back in, and the resulting 4% wine can be used as a blending component to add to untreated wine, to result in a final wine at a lower alcohol level.

How did the wines taste? I started off looking at a Californian Chardonnay at 14.3% alcohol. It had a sweet, ripe, slightly buttery nose, leading to a rich buttery palate that was quite broad. I then tasted the same wine after it had been through the spinning cone column, at 4% alcohol. This was more minerally with tangerine notes and some spicy richness. The palate was lemony and tart with hollow fruit and an enhanced sensation of acidity. Their winemaker told me that alcohol is a masking agent so taking it away reveals what’s there. It also adds sweetness to the palate. Also, the acidity is concentrated, and appears higher up in the mix. I guess what this showed is that it really matters what you start off with, when you start taking alcohol out. But also that it has a huge effect on flavour.

The next wine was a blend of 10% of the 4% sample with the remainder of the original wine, resulting in a Chardonnay at 13.2%. This was fresher than the original with more acidity apparent. The fruit showed through more. There was quite a difference, and the 13.2% wine was much nicer than the 14.3% original.

I then tried four different Californian wines each at three alcohol levels: the original level, and then reduced levels of 11% and 8%. A Chardonnay that tasted sweet and buttery at 14% alcohol tasted fresher with nice definition at 11%, and then more lemony and refreshing at 8%. A rosé showed best at 12.2%, and was perhaps less successful at 8%. A Shiraz was sweet, juicy and spicy at 14.6%, but fresher and more vivid with less sweetness at 11%; at 8% it was more savoury with fresh, pure fruit and a more gastronomic character. A Merlot showed really well at 11% and fresh, juicy and bracing with more apparent acidity at 8%. These are inexpensive wines, but with this alcohol reduction they really showed very well.

What was immediately apparent was the role that alcohol has in shaping the flavour and aroma of the wine. Take just a little out, and you have a different wine. But in the region of 8% alcohol and above, you can make some very interesting wines, depending on your starting wine.

But my experience of zero alcohol wine has been quite different. Remove it all, and you have something that really doesn’t taste all that wine like at all. This is for three reasons. First, the alcohol itself is contributing something important to the flavour. It adds some sweetness and richness, and quite a lot of the body. And second, alcohol is acting as a masking agent. We like wines the way they taste, but without alcohol and its masking, suddenly you reveal all sorts of aromas that you didn’t see before. And it smells and tastes different, and a bit weird.

It’s not possible to neatly take off all the aroma compounds in one fraction, then take off the alcohol in a second, and then combine back the aroma compounds. This is because many of the desirable aroma compounds leave in the alcohol stream. The evidence in the scientific literature shows that many of the interesting aroma compounds are lost in the dealcoholization process.

Also, there are significant changes in acidity. For example, one study showed that a white wine where the original level was 6.88 g/L rose to 10.05 g/L in the dealcoholized wine and pH lowers with this from 3.00 to 2.70). This is taking these parameters out of the normal range for table wines.

With much more work on technology, it may be possible to preserve more of the aroma molecules in the wine than is currently possible. But this won’t overcome the second, larger problem faced by non-alcoholic wines – the importance of the non-volatile matrix on aroma release.

But for now, it seems that eliminating alcohol changes so much in a wine that it’s very hard to end up with anything that tastes like wine. For most zero-alcohol wines, it’s normal to add sugar at a level of around 40 g/litre, and the resulting wine doesn’t taste sweet, largely because of the sky-high acidity. But this sort of ultraprocessed wine is sort of at odds with where we are heading in terms of gastronomy at the moment.

I remain optimistic about wines that have just a little alcohol reduced, though. Going from 15% to 12% might be a good thing, or going from 13% to 10%, especially for more commercial styles. Sometimes, picking earlier does this job without intervention. But I’m open to some intervention if the results are good.

  • Jamie Goode is a London-based wine writer, lecturer, wine judge and book author. With a PhD in plant biology, he worked as a science editor, before starting wineanorak.com, one of the world’s most popular wine websites.
